newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy 1997 budget needs extra spending cuts - court.
newsitem.headline: Italy 1997 budget needs extra spending cuts - court.

text.p: Italy's 1997 budget in itself will not be enough to rebalance state accounts and will have to be linked to structural spending cuts, the head of the Court of Accounts said.
Giuseppe Carbone, chairman of the court which oversees state accounts, was addressing a parliamentary budget commission.

Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio on Thursday cautiously welcomed the 1997 budget but warned it might not be enough to meet the tough criteria set for founder members of the European single currency.
Also addressing the budget commission, he cautioned that the austerity budget, designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire off next year's deficit, could hurt sluggish economic growth.
The Court said it believed "a complete rethink of the rules and levels of state social services" was necessary.
Referring specifically to the health and pensions sectors, Carbone said the government should be given carte blanche by parliament in order to take the necessary measures in the first half of 1997.

Such cuts in expenditure could not be put put off until the 1998 budget as this would result in an "unbearable decision-making overload" in the final run-up to single European currency deadlines, according to the Court.
Even if such measures were carried out the Court believed they still might not be enough to keep to Maastricht parameters.
But, Carbone said, it was in any case preferable "to get rigorous structural action underway urgently", rather than "resort to quantitative objectives through mere accounting adjustments."

Even if Italy failed to fully comply with Maastricht criteria, the Court believed, structural intervention on spending would give a signal to its European partners that the country was making serious efforts to restore state finances to health.
